The Bald notothen Pagothenia borchgrevinki is a cryopelagic nototheniid endemic to the high-latitude waters of Antarctica, where it occupies the sub-ice platelet layer and feeds predominantly on krill and copepods. This species attains an ultimate total length of 28 centimeters [Li = 28 centimeters], placing it among the smaller nototheniids of McMurdo Sound. Body mass increases rapidly during the juvenile growth phase, and individuals reach a wet weight at birth of just 0.036 grams [Wwb = 0.036 grams], a value consistent with the small egg size typical of this lineage. Such a diminutive starting mass imposes high vulnerability to predation during the early larval stages, and the hatchlings must develop rapidly to become effective foragers.

At the frigid temperatures characteristic of its environment, the onset of sexual maturity is tightly constrained. Field collections indicate that the total length at puberty is approximately 15.2 centimeters [Lp = approximately 15.2 centimeters], a length that corresponds roughly to the transition from sub-adult to adult feeding ecology. Individuals reaching this size have accrued sufficient somatic reserves to support gonadal development. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is 38.4 grams [Wwp = 38.4 grams], derived from the length-weight relationship typical of the species, and this mass threshold appears to be a reliable proxy for the initiation of gametogenesis in both sexes.

Reproductive output in Pagothenia borchgrevinki is closely tied to the stable but extreme thermal regime of the Southern Ocean. Under water temperatures of -1.7 °C [T = -1.7 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is achieved through the production of a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with each spawning event yielding approximately 3000 eggs [N_R_i = each spawning event yielding approximately 3000 eggs]. This low fecundity is offset by the prolonged parental investment in large, yolk-rich eggs, and the species displays a typical K-selected life history strategy common among Antarctic nototheniids.

Embryonic development proceeds slowly under the near-freezing conditions of the benthic environment. Eggs incubated at a stable temperature of 0 °C [T = 0 °C] require an extended incubation period of 95 days [ab = 95 days] before hatching occurs, a duration that is considerably longer than that of temperate teleosts with comparable egg sizes. This protracted embryonic phase reflects the extreme cold adaptation of the species and results in the emergence of relatively well-developed yolk-sac larvae that possess sufficient endogenous reserves to begin exogenous feeding within a few days.

Longevity in this species is notable given its small body size. The maximum lifespan in the wild has been estimated at 20 years [am = 20 years] at -1.7 °C [T = -1.7 °C], reflecting the slow growth and delayed maturation characteristic of Antarctic fishes. The ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown adult is 272.7 grams [Wwi = 272.7 grams], a mass that approaches the upper size limit for cryopelagic nototheniids in McMurdo Sound and reflects the species' adaptation to the extreme thermal constraints of its environment. Such a decelerated life pace, with late puberty, negligible annual reproductive output, and extraordinary longevity, aligns well with the predictions of the metabolic theory of ecology for organisms living at extremely low environmental temperatures.
